steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A comparator compares two input voltages and switches its output to indicate which is higher; no negative feedback is used.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: When V+ > V−, the output goes to positive saturation; when V+ < V−, the output goes to negative saturation.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A simple comparator has a single threshold voltage; the output switches when the input crosses this level.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Noise on the input signal can cause a simple comparator to chatter (switch rapidly) near the threshold.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Explain why a simple comparator can produce a chattering output when the input signal is noisy. | Q: A Schmitt trigger has V_UT = 4 V and V_LT = 2 V. What is the hysteresis voltage? | Q: State the role of positive feedback in a Schmitt trigger.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Noise causes the input to cross the single threshold repeatedly, making the output switch rapidly between states. | V_H = V_UT − V_LT = 4 − 2 = 2 V. | Positive feedback creates two distinct threshold voltages (hysteresis), accelerates switching transitions and eliminates output chatter.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When drawing a Schmitt trigger, clearly show the positive feedback resistor from output to non-inverting input. Label both threshold voltages (V_UT and V_LT) on the transfer characteristic and state the hysteresis value. Explain hysteresis using the analogy: the output 'remembers' its previous state until the opposite threshold is crossed. For calculations, always state the hysteresis formula: V_H = V_UT − V_LT. Distinguish between a simple comparator (one threshold) and a Schmitt trigger (two thresholds with hysteresis).
